sections.title: Structure of a Typical Long Bone

blocks.name: Bone (osseous tissue)
blocks.def: A hard, dense <term d="The tissue that supports, binds and separates other tissues, rich in matrix between its cells.">connective tissue</term> that forms most of the adult skeleton. The skeletal system includes all the bones, cartilages, and ligaments. The adult skeleton has 206 bones.

blocks.x: Bone tissue differs greatly from other body tissues: it is hard, and many of its functions depend on that hardness — yet it is also dynamic, adjusting its shape to accommodate mechanical stress.
Functions of the Skeletal System

items: Support — a hard framework that supports and anchors the soft organs of the body.
Protection — surrounds organs such as the brain and spinal cord.
Movement — allows for muscle attachment, so bones act as levers.
Storage — minerals (calcium) and lipids are stored within bone material.
Blood cell formation — bone marrow is responsible for blood cell production.
Hormone production — bones produce osteocalcin, which helps regulate bone formation.

blocks.x: The 206 bones of the adult skeleton are divided into five shape-based categories, each with a distinct function.

blocks.cap: The five shape categories of bone: long, short, flat, sesamoid, and irregular.

blocks.name: Long bones
blocks.def: Typically longer than wide (tubular); have a shaft with heads at both ends; contain mostly <term d="The dense, solid outer layer of bone that gives it strength.">compact bone</term>. Function as levers, moving when muscles contract. Examples: femur, humerus, radius, ulna, tibia, fibula.

blocks.name: Short bones
blocks.def: Generally cube-shaped; contain mostly <term d="The lighter, honeycombed bone found inside the ends of long bones.">spongy bone</term>. Provide stability and support, with some limited motion. Examples: carpals, tarsals.

blocks.name: Flat bones
blocks.def: Thin and flattened, usually curved; thin layers of compact bone around a layer of spongy bone. Serve as muscle attachment points and often protect internal organs. Examples: skull, ribs, sternum.

blocks.name: Irregular bones
blocks.def: Irregular in shape; don't fit into the other categories. Examples: vertebrae, hip bone.

blocks.name: Sesamoid bones
blocks.def: Small, round bones shaped like a sesame seed. Form within tendons where a great deal of pressure is generated at a joint, protecting the <term d="A strong cord of fibrous tissue that attaches muscle to bone.">tendon</term> by helping it overcome compressive forces. Example: patella.

sections.title: Structure of a Typical Long Bone

blocks.name: <term d="The widened end of a long bone, taking part in the joint.">Epiphysis</term>
blocks.def: The end(s) of a bone; contains red marrow; mostly spongy (cancellous/trabecular) bone.

blocks.name: <term d="The long shaft of a long bone.">Diaphysis</term>
blocks.def: The "shaft" of a bone; made of compact bone; has a medullary cavity containing yellow marrow (a storage site for triglycerides).

blocks.name: <term d="The region between the shaft and the end of a long bone, where growth happens.">Metaphysis</term>
blocks.def: The region where the diaphysis and epiphysis meet. Contains the cartilaginous epiphyseal (growth) plate — the actively growing region of a long bone during childhood/adolescence.

blocks.name: Articular <term d="A firm but flexible connective tissue that cushions joints and shapes structures like the ear.">cartilage</term>
blocks.def: A thin layer of hyaline cartilage covering each epiphysis, cushioning the joint surface.

blocks.name: <term d="The tough membrane wrapping the outer surface of a bone, carrying its blood supply.">Periosteum</term>
blocks.def: A thick connective tissue layer covering the outer surfaces of bone (except at articular surfaces, sesamoid bones, and ossicles), attached to the underlying bone by <term d="A strong rope-like protein fibre that gives tissues their tensile strength.">collagen</term> (Sharpey's) fibers. Osteogenic — critical for fracture repair, so much so that bone stripped of its periosteum will not survive. Richly supplied with pain-sensitive nerve fibers.

blocks.name: <term d="The thin lining on the inner surfaces of bone, facing the marrow cavity.">Endosteum</term>
blocks.def: A thin, vascular connective tissue membrane lining the inner (medullary) surface of bone. Single-layered; also covers the trabeculae of spongy bone and lines the central canals of osteons. Osteogenic, contributing to new bone formation.

blocks.x: The most common sites for bone marrow aspiration are the manubrium sterni in adults and the iliac crest in children.
Bone Cells

blocks.name: Osteoblasts
blocks.def: Bone-building cells that secrete the organic matrix (osteoid) of bone.

blocks.name: Osteocytes
blocks.def: Mature bone cells — former osteoblasts trapped within the bone matrix they secreted; maintain bone tissue.

blocks.name: Osteoclasts
blocks.def: Large, multinucleate cells that resorb (break down) bone tissue, releasing stored minerals.

blocks.x: Compact vs. Spongy Bone

blocks.name: Osteons (Haversian systems)
blocks.def: The structural units of compact bone — concentric rings (lamellae) of bone matrix around a central (Haversian) canal that carries blood vessels and nerves.

blocks.name: Spongy (cancellous) bone
blocks.def: An open lattice of bony spikes called trabeculae, with spaces filled by red bone marrow. Lighter than compact bone but still resists stress from many directions.

blocks.name: Osteogenesis (<term d="The process by which new bone is formed.">ossification</term>)
blocks.def: The process of bone formation. Occurs via two pathways: intramembranous ossification (bone forms directly from mesenchyme — e.g. flat bones of the skull) and endochondral ossification (bone replaces a pre-existing hyaline cartilage model — e.g. most of the skeleton).

blocks.name: Bone repair (fracture healing)
blocks.def: Proceeds through defined stages: hematoma formation, fibrocartilaginous (soft) callus formation, bony (hard) callus formation, and finally bone remodeling.

blocks.x: Role of Hormones in Bone

blocks.name: Growth hormone
blocks.def: Produced by the pituitary; stimulates bone growth generally.

blocks.name: Thyroid hormone
blocks.def: Regulates the rate of bone growth and maturation.

blocks.name: Parathyroid hormone (PTH)
blocks.def: Raises blood calcium by stimulating <term d="A large cell that breaks bone down, releasing its minerals.">osteoclast</term> activity (bone resorption) when calcium levels are low.

blocks.name: Calcitonin
blocks.def: Lowers blood calcium by inhibiting osteoclast activity.

blocks.name: Sex hormones (estrogen/testosterone)
blocks.def: Promote the growth spurt at puberty and later contribute to closure of the epiphyseal plates.

blocks.name: Osteoporosis
blocks.def: A condition of decreased bone density/mass, making bones fragile and prone to fracture. Women lose bone mass faster than men after menopause (roughly 8% per decade vs. 3% in men).

blocks.name: Osteopenia
blocks.def: A decreased calcification of bone, or reduced bone mass, due to inadequate osteoid synthesis — considered a precursor stage to osteoporosis.

blocks.name: Vitamin D deficiency
blocks.def: Impairs calcium absorption in the gut, leading to poor bone mineralization — causes rickets in children and osteomalacia in adults.

blocks.name: Gigantism & Acromegaly
blocks.def: Both caused by excess growth hormone. Gigantism occurs if the excess happens before the epiphyseal (growth) plates close, causing excessive height. Acromegaly occurs after the plates have closed, causing thickening of bones in the hands, feet, and face rather than increased height.

blocks.name: Achondroplasia
blocks.def: The most common form of dwarfism, caused by a genetic defect affecting cartilage-to-bone conversion at the growth plates, resulting in short limbs with a relatively normal-sized trunk.

blocks.name: Marfan's syndrome
blocks.def: A genetic disorder of connective tissue affecting the skeleton (as well as the heart and eyes), often producing unusually long limbs and digits.

blocks.name: Paget's disease
blocks.def: Excessive bone breakdown coupled with abnormal, disorganized bone formation, resulting in a high proportion of weak, woven bone.

blocks.name: Club foot
blocks.def: A congenital defect in which the soles of the foot face medially and the talus points inferiorly.

blocks.x: Bone markings are surface features that indicate where bones interact with other structures — where tendons/ligaments attach, or where nerves and blood vessels pass. They fall into two broad categories:

blocks.name: Depressions & openings
blocks.def: Foramen (a rounded/oval opening through a bone), fossa (a shallow basin), sulcus (a groove), meatus (a canal-like passage), fissure (a narrow slit-like opening) — allow the passage of soft tissue, e.g. nerves and blood vessels.

blocks.name: Projections & processes
blocks.def: Tuberosity (a large rounded projection), tubercle (a small rounded projection), spine (a sharp, slender projection), crest (a narrow ridge of bone), condyle (a rounded articular projection), ramus (an arm-like projection), neck (a narrowed structure supporting the head), trochanter (a large, blunt projection found only on the femur) — sites of muscle/<term d="A tough band of fibrous tissue that joins one bone to another.">ligament</term> attachment or joint formation.

blocks.cap: Common bone markings and surface features referenced throughout <term d="The branch of anatomy that studies bones.">osteology</term>.

blocks.x: The axial skeleton forms the central axis of the body — the skull, vertebral column, and thoracic cage — and, together with the appendicular skeleton (126 bones), makes up the 206 named bones of the adult skeleton. At birth there are about 270 bones; the number decreases with age as separate bones gradually fuse together.
The Cranium — 8 Bones
The cranium has a vault (calvaria/skullcap) and a base/floor. Internally, prominent bony ridges divide the cranial base into three fossae — anterior, middle, and posterior.

blocks.name: Cranial bones
blocks.def: 8 bones total. Paired: temporal bones, parietal bones. Unpaired: frontal bone, occipital bone, sphenoid bone, ethmoid bone. Memory aid: "Old People From Timbuktu Eat Spiders" — Occipital, Parietal, Frontal, Temporal, Ethmoid, Sphenoid, sometimes shortened to "PEST OF 6."

blocks.cap: Lateral view of the skull, showing the cranial and facial bones.

blocks.x: ▶️Watch: The SkullA walkthrough of the cranial and facial bones, sutures, and key landmarks covered above.
Parietal Bones & the Sutures of the Skull

blocks.name: Coronal suture
blocks.def: Where the parietal bones meet the frontal bone anteriorly.

blocks.name: <term d="Flat, scale-like in shape — used to describe thin, plate-shaped cells.">Squamous</term> suture
blocks.def: Where a parietal and temporal bone meet on the lateral skull.

blocks.name: Sagittal suture
blocks.def: Where the parietal bones meet superiorly at the cranial midline.

blocks.name: Lambdoid suture
blocks.def: Where the parietal bones meet the occipital bone posteriorly.

blocks.name: Bregma & Lambda
blocks.def: Bregma is the point where the sagittal and coronal sutures meet. Lambda is the point where the sagittal and lambdoid sutures meet.

blocks.name: Calvaria (inferior aspect features)
blocks.def: Vascular grooves for branches of the middle meningeal artery; granular foveolae (pits formed by arachnoid granulations, where CSF is transferred into venous blood); a groove for the superior sagittal sinus (a large venous channel within the dura mater); and the diploë (a layer of cancellous bone between the inner and outer tables of the skull, containing red marrow).

blocks.x: The Ethmoid Bone

blocks.name: Ethmoid bone
blocks.def: Located on the midline in the anterior cranial floor, medial to the orbits. A major superior supporting structure of the nasal cavity. Contains thin, scroll-like projections called conchae, lined by mucous membrane — the increased surface area helps humidify inhaled air and trap particles.

blocks.x: The Three Cranial Fossae

blocks.name: Anterior cranial fossa
blocks.def: Houses the frontal lobes of the brain. Formed by the orbital portion of the frontal bone, the ethmoid bone in the middle, and the lesser wing of the sphenoid. Features include the frontal crest, the foramen caecum at its base (for developmental vessel passage), and the crista galli (a superior ethmoid ridge anchoring the cerebral falx).

blocks.name: Middle cranial fossa
blocks.def: Houses the temporal lobes of the brain. Formed by the greater wing of the sphenoid and the squamous/petrous portions of the temporal bone. Centered on the sella turcica ("Turkish saddle"), flanked by the anterior and posterior clinoid processes.

blocks.name: Sella turcica
blocks.def: A saddle-shaped bony formation on the sphenoid body with three parts — the hypophyseal (pituitary) fossa, tuberculum sellae, and dorsum sellae — housing and protecting the pituitary gland. A fall/head injury can fracture this region and damage the pituitary.

blocks.name: Posterior cranial fossa
blocks.def: The largest and deepest of the three fossae; houses the cerebellum, pons, and medulla. Formed mainly by the occipital bone and the petrous/mastoid portions of the temporal bone. Features the clivus, the foramen magnum, and the internal occipital crest/protuberance.

blocks.x: The Orbit & Facial Bones

blocks.name: Bones of the orbit
blocks.def: Seven bones articulate to form each bony eye socket: the frontal, zygomatic, maxillary, lacrimal, ethmoid, palatine, and sphenoid bones.

blocks.name: Facial bones (14)
blocks.def: Include the maxillae (upper jaw), the mandible (lower jaw — U-shaped, houses the lower teeth, the only mobile bone of the skull), the zygomatic bones (cheekbones), nasal bones, lacrimal bones, palatine bones, inferior nasal conchae, and the vomer (part of the nasal septum).

blocks.name: Paranasal sinuses
blocks.def: Air-filled spaces within the frontal, ethmoid, sphenoid, and maxillary bones that lighten the skull and add resonance to the voice.

blocks.name: Cleft lip/palate
blocks.def: A congenital defect from incomplete fusion of the facial processes/palatine structures during development.

blocks.x: Fontanelles

blocks.name: Fontanelles ("little fountains")
blocks.def: The unossified, membranous gaps between an infant's cranial bones. Allow the skull to compress slightly during birth and accommodate rapid brain growth in infancy; useful clinical landmarks for assessing hydration/intracranial pressure. Gradually ossify and close over the first two years of life.

blocks.x: The Vertebral Column (Spine)
The vertebral column has 5 regions with characteristic normal curvatures: cervical (7), thoracic (12), lumbar (5), sacral (5 fused), and coccygeal (3–4 fused).

blocks.cap: Structure of a typical (thoracic) vertebra, showing the body, vertebral arch, and processes.

blocks.x: ▶️Watch: The Vertebral ColumnRegions, curvatures, and the structure of a typical vertebra, shown in 3D.

blocks.name: Typical vertebra (structure)
blocks.def: Consists of a body (anteriorly) and a vertebral (neural) arch that together enclose the vertebral foramen. The arch is made of pedicles (projecting from the body) and laminae (which unite to form the spinous process). Transverse processes project laterally, and articular facets allow <term d="A joint — the place where two bones meet.">articulation</term> with adjacent vertebrae.

blocks.name: Atlas (C1)
blocks.def: Lacks a body and spinous process; its superior articular facets form the atlanto-occipital joint with the occipital condyles (a condyloid joint permitting the head to "nod yes").

blocks.name: Axis (C2)
blocks.def: Has a peg-like dens (odontoid process) that articulates with the atlas as a pivot joint, secured by the transverse ligament, permitting rotation of the head ("shaking the head no").

blocks.name: C7 (vertebra prominens)
blocks.def: Has an unusually long spinous process and is used as a landmark for counting vertebral levels.

blocks.name: Thoracic vertebrae (T1–T12)
blocks.def: Medium-sized, heart-shaped bodies, concave forward, with long spines inclined downward. Bear costal facets on the body (where rib heads articulate) and, except T11–T12, on the transverse processes too (rib tubercles). T1 and T9–T12 are atypical; the rest are typical.

blocks.name: Lumbar vertebrae (L1–L5)
blocks.def: Large, kidney-shaped bodies; a triangular vertebral foramen; short, strong, posterolateral pedicles; and an almost horizontal, quadrangular, thickened spinous process — built for weight-bearing rather than rotation.

blocks.name: Sacrum
blocks.def: Large and triangular, located at the upper/posterior pelvic cavity with a narrow, blunt apex; articulates with the pelvic girdle and the coccyx. The male sacrum is shorter, narrower, and more curved than the wider, flatter female sacrum (an adaptation for childbirth).

blocks.name: Coccyx
blocks.def: A small triangular bone formed by four rudimentary fused vertebral segments, directed downward and ventrally, with rudimentary transverse processes.

blocks.name: Intervertebral discs
blocks.def: Fibrocartilage cushions between vertebral bodies that act as shock absorbers, accounting for 20–25% of the total height of the vertebral column. Absent between C1–C2 and within the fused sacrum/coccyx. Composed of an inner, gel-like nucleus pulposus and an outer, fibrous annulus fibrosus.

blocks.name: Herniated (slipped/prolapsed) disc
blocks.def: Rupture of the annulus fibrosus followed by protrusion of the nucleus pulposus, which may compress the spinal cord, cauda equina, or spinal nerves. Typically occurs posterolaterally, most often at L4–L5 or L5–S1, and may cause sciatica.

blocks.name: Spondylolisthesis
blocks.def: A fracture/defect of the vertebral column (classically at L4/L5) where the spine, laminae, and inferior articular processes separate from the rest of the vertebra. Caused by falls onto the feet or diving head-first; presents with lower back pain.

blocks.name: Spina bifida
blocks.def: A congenital defect where the vertebral laminae fail to unite, most common in the lumbosacral region; associated with maternal folic acid deficiency in genetically susceptible individuals; treated surgically.

blocks.name: Abnormal spinal curvatures
blocks.def: Scoliosis (abnormal lateral curvature), kyphosis (excessive thoracic curvature, "hunchback"), and lordosis (excessive lumbar curvature, "swayback").

blocks.x: The Thoracic Cage

blocks.name: Sternum
blocks.def: Has three parts: the manubrium (superior part, articulating with the clavicles and the first two rib pairs), the body (the bulk of the sternum, notched at its sides for costal cartilage of ribs 2–7), and the xiphoid process (the inferior tip, which may be bifid or perforated).

blocks.name: True, false & floating ribs
blocks.def: Ribs 1–7 are "true ribs" (attach directly to the sternum via costal cartilage); ribs 8–10 are "false ribs" (attach indirectly, via the cartilage of the rib above); ribs 11–12 are "floating ribs" (no anterior attachment at all).

blocks.x: The appendicular skeleton comprises the bones of the limbs and the girdles that attach them to the axial skeleton.
Upper Limb

blocks.name: Pectoral (shoulder) girdle
blocks.def: The scapula (shoulder blade) and clavicle (collar bone), attaching the upper limb to the axial skeleton.

blocks.x: ▶️Watch: The ScapulaLandmarks and articulations of the shoulder blade.

blocks.name: Humerus
blocks.def: The single bone of the arm, articulating with the scapula at the shoulder and with the radius and ulna at the elbow. Divided into a <term d="Nearer to the trunk or to the point where a limb attaches.">proximal</term> end, body (shaft), and <term d="Further away from the trunk or from the point where a limb attaches.">distal</term> end. The proximal end bears the head, the anatomical neck, and two tubercles (greater and lesser) separated by the intertubercular groove/sulcus. Joins the shaft at the surgical neck — a common fracture site where the axillary nerve can be injured. The shaft bears the deltoid tuberosity laterally and the radial (spiral) groove posteriorly, carrying the radial nerve — mid-shaft fractures classically cause radial nerve injury (wrist drop).

blocks.cap: The humerus, the single long bone of the upper arm.

blocks.x: ▶️Watch: The HumerusProximal and distal landmarks of the arm bone, including the surgical neck and radial groove.

blocks.name: Radius & ulna
blocks.def: The two bones of the forearm (antebrachium); the radius is lateral (thumb side), the ulna is medial.

blocks.x: ▶️Watch: The Radius and UlnaForearm bone landmarks and how they articulate at the elbow and wrist.

blocks.name: Carpal bones (carpus)
blocks.def: 8 wrist bones in two rows of four. Most bear articular facets except the pisiform; the hamate has a distinctive hook; the scaphoid is the most frequently fractured carpal, with tenderness at the anatomical snuffbox (floored by the scaphoid and trapezium).

blocks.name: Carpal bone mnemonic
blocks.def: Proximal row (lateral to medial): Scaphoid, Lunate, Triquetrum, Pisiform. Distal row (lateral to medial): Trapezium, Trapezoid, Capitate, Hamate. Combined: "So Luke Took Peter, To The Church Hall."

blocks.name: Carpal tunnel syndrome
blocks.def: Compression of the median nerve as it passes through the carpal tunnel (formed by the carpal bones and flexor retinaculum), causing pain, numbness, and tingling in the hand.

blocks.name: Metacarpals & phalanges
blocks.def: Metacarpals numbered 1–5 (thumb/pollex = 1); their bases articulate with the carpal bones. Phalanges: proximal, middle, and distal in each finger, except the thumb (proximal and distal only).

blocks.x: ▶️Watch: Bones of the HandThe carpals, metacarpals, and phalanges, including the carpal bone mnemonic in action.
Lower Limb

blocks.name: Pelvic girdle (bony pelvis)
blocks.def: A bony ring composed of the sacrum and the right/left hip bones, joined anteriorly at the pubic symphysis. Transfers body weight from the vertebral column, through the sacroiliac and hip joints, to the femurs.

blocks.name: Os coxae (hip bone)
blocks.def: Formed by fusion of the ilium, ischium, and pubis at the acetabulum (which receives the femoral head). Fusion progresses from a Y-shaped triradiate cartilage at puberty to complete bony fusion by 20–25 years of age.

blocks.name: Ilium
blocks.def: The largest, uppermost hip bone; has a body (forming 2/5 of the acetabulum) and an ala (wing).

blocks.name: Ischium
blocks.def: The postero-inferior hip bone; its free lower end forms the ischial tuberosity, which bears body weight while sitting (and can develop ischial bursitis).

blocks.name: Pubis
blocks.def: The anterior hip bone; divided into a body and two rami. Its roughened anterior border is the pubic crest; its lower lateral part is the pubic tubercle, an abdominal wall landmark.

blocks.name: Obturator foramen
blocks.def: A large opening bounded by the pubis, ischium, and their rami, closed by the obturator membrane except at the obturator groove.

blocks.name: Male vs. female pelvis
blocks.def: The female pelvis has a wider, more circular inlet, an enlarged outlet, less sacral/coccygeal curvature, and a broader pubic angle (>100°) — all adaptations for childbirth.

blocks.name: Femur (thigh bone)
blocks.def: The longest, heaviest bone in the body (roughly 1/4–1/3 of body height); transmits weight from the hip bone to the tibia while standing. Upper end bears the head, neck, and two trochanters (greater and lesser); lower end bears two condyles (medial and lateral) separated by the intercondylar fossa.

blocks.name: Patella
blocks.def: The kneecap, a sesamoid bone embedded in the quadriceps tendon.

blocks.name: Tibia & fibula
blocks.def: The two bones of the leg (shin); the tibia is the main weight-bearing bone, the fibula is thinner and mainly for muscle attachment.

blocks.cap: The distal end of the tibia, forming part of the ankle joint.

blocks.x: ▶️Watch: The Tibia and FibulaLeg bone landmarks and their role in forming the ankle joint.

blocks.name: Tarsal bones
blocks.def: 7 bones of the ankle, including the talus (articulates with the tibia/fibula) and the calcaneus (heel bone, the largest tarsal).

blocks.name: Metatarsals & phalanges (foot)
blocks.def: The bones of the sole and toes, numbered 1–5, structurally similar to the metacarpals/phalanges of the hand.

blocks.x: ▶️Watch: Bones of the FootThe tarsals, metatarsals, and phalanges, and how the foot's arches are formed.

blocks.name: Arches of the foot
blocks.def: The medial longitudinal, lateral longitudinal, and transverse arches distribute body weight and provide spring while walking/running.
